articles.title: Heatwave hits five provinces as temperatures soar to 38°C - Inside Metros

articles.full_text:
Staff Reporter
The South African Weather Service (SAWS) has warned of heatwave conditions across five provinces on Thursday and Friday, with temperatures expected to reach 38°C in parts of the country.
The warning covers north-eastern parts of the Northern Cape, North West, most of the Free State, Gauteng and parts of southern and south-western Limpopo.
Some of the highest temperatures on Thursday are expected in Kimberley, Mahikeng, Upington and Vryburg, where maximums could reach 38°C. Bloemfontein is forecast to reach 37°C.
Gauteng will also experience intense heat, with Pretoria expected to reach 34°C on Thursday and 35°C on Friday. Johannesburg’s maximum temperature is forecast to rise from 32°C to 33°C over the same period.

SAWS has also warned of extremely high fire danger conditions across much of the Northern Cape, Free State, western North West, parts of the Joe Gqabi district in the Eastern Cape and the Matzikama municipality in the Western Cape.
While much of the country’s interior will remain hot to very hot, coastal areas are expected to experience milder conditions, with showers and rain forecast for parts of KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape.
Isolated afternoon showers and thundershowers are expected in northern Gauteng and north-eastern North West on Thursday, with further thunderstorms possible over eastern parts of the country on Friday.
Temperatures across major metros
In Johannesburg, temperatures are forecast to range between 17°C and 32°C on Thursday, rising to between 19°C and 33°C on Friday.
Tshwane is expected to record a minimum of 19°C and a maximum of 34°C on Thursday, followed by 21°C and 35°C on Friday.
In Mangaung, which includes Bloemfontein, temperatures are forecast to range between 17°C and 37°C on Thursday and between 16°C and 36°C on Friday.
Coastal metros will experience considerably cooler conditions.
In eThekwini, Durban is expected to record temperatures between 20°C and 25°C on Thursday, followed by 21°C and 24°C on Friday, with showers forecast.
Cape Town will see temperatures ranging from 17°C to 24°C on Thursday, dropping to between 15°C and 20°C on Friday.
In Nelson Mandela Bay, Gqeberha is forecast to record a minimum of 17°C and a maximum of 23°C on Thursday, followed by 16°C and 21°C on Friday.
Buffalo City, which includes East London, can expect temperatures between 18°C and 23°C on Thursday and between 17°C and 20°C on Friday, with showers possible.
A separate forecast for Ekurhuleni could not be verified.
Heat poses health and fire risks
SAWS has warned that prolonged exposure to high temperatures could increase the risk of dehydration, heat exhaustion and heatstroke, particularly among children, older people and those working outdoors.
Residents in affected areas have been advised to drink water regularly, avoid strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest parts of the day and remain in shaded or well-ventilated areas.
The weather service has also urged residents to exercise caution in areas experiencing extreme fire danger conditions, where dry vegetation and high temperatures could allow veld fires to spread quickly.
Despite the possibility of isolated thunderstorms in some inland areas, heatwave conditions are expected to persist into Friday.

Gauteng residents have been urged to use water sparingly as persistent heatwave conditions increase demand and place additional pressure on water supply systems.
Residents have been urged to use water sparingly as the persistent heatwave called the El Niño phenomenon drives up water demand across Gauteng municipalities.
According to the Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS), the heatwave will continue to place additional pressure on water supply systems during the 2026/27 summer season.
The department warns that excessive water use in areas with a reliable supply could worsen shortages in areas already experiencing water supply disruptions.
“This is compounding existing challenges, particularly substantial water losses through leaking municipal distribution infrastructure and high average consumption per capita in certain areas,” the department said.
In Midvaal, Municipal Manager Phumudzo Magodi informed residents about the implementation of restrictions by Rand Water, citing that current water consumption in Gauteng is well above the available design capacity of the bulk water supply infrastructure, placing a serious strain on the system and affecting Rand Water’s storage levels.
“To mitigate the situation and protect the regional water supply system, Rand Water has implemented a 25% restriction on municipal bulk water supply meters. This sudden, drastic reduction of water supply by Rand Water has negatively impacted the Municipality’s ability to supply water sustainably,” Magodi said.
The municipality said water supply will continue even though residents are experiencing reduced water pressure, particularly during peak consumption periods.
“Certain areas, including Klipwater and Henley on Klip, are already experiencing low water pressure and intermittent water supply interruptions. Residents are requested to report instances of no water or prolonged supply interruptions through the Municipality’s official reporting channels to enable appropriate intervention measures.
The municipality urged residents, businesses, industries, and institutions to use water responsibly and implement water-saving measures wherever possible.
“Reducing non-essential water consumption is critical to easing pressure on the system and ensuring the continued availability of water for all consumers. The Municipality will continue to monitor the situation closely in collaboration with Rand Water and other relevant stakeholders and will provide updates as further information becomes available.”
Municipalities have been encouraged to keep communities regularly informed about the status of their water supply systems, including treatment and distribution capacity, supply constraints and interventions that could affect availability.
The department said consistent and timely communication will help residents understand prevailing conditions, plan accordingly and make informed decisions about their water use.
“Where necessary, DWS will implement reductions in authorised water abstraction by agricultural, industrial and other water users, including water boards, to protect stressed water resources.”
Lebo Chaha is a journalist for Sedibeng Ster and Ster North. She is mostly passionate about stories that bring positive change in her community. Email: lebo@mooivaal.co.za

The Charles depression has already crossed Madeira and is currently, at 10 am, making its way towards mainland Portugal. “The latest numerical models point to a reduction in the intensity of the wind and gusts,” IPMA meteorologist Patrícia Gomes told Lusa.
“The depression ended up changing its characteristics and is not producing as much wind,” she added, stressing that a scenario similar to the one experienced in central Portugal earlier this year with Storm Kristin has been “largely ruled out”.
Patrícia Gomes explained these changes: “The centre of the depression will not have as low atmospheric pressure as previously forecast, and that makes all the difference to wind intensity and the severity of meteorological parameters.”
The country has been under a state of alert since midnight on 11 November due to the passage of the Charles depression, which initially hit the Autonomous Region of Madeira.
Heavy rainfall is still forecast for mainland Portugal, but “the wind has decreased in intensity and gust strength, resulting in a downgrade of the warning level for gusts”.
Only the district of Faro remains under a red warning for gusts, which could reach 120 km/h and, in the most exposed areas, up to 140 km/h.
In the districts of Lisbon, Setúbal and Beja, gusts of 100 km/h are forecast, potentially reaching 120 km/h in the most exposed areas, such as higher mountain ranges and coastal areas.
The remaining districts in Alentejo and central Portugal are under yellow gust warnings, with winds estimated at 90 km/h.
“The warning for Lisbon was brought forward and downgraded,” Patrícia Gomes added, saying that warnings in the districts of Lisbon, Setúbal and Faro will remain in place until 6 pm.
Regarding rainfall in these districts, red precipitation warnings remain in place, with only Évora downgraded to orange. “These warnings end at 6 pm in the southernmost parts of the country, while in the north they end at 9 pm,” the meteorologist added, stressing that further adjustments may be made throughout the day.
Forecasts of worsening weather conditions prompted the Government to decide to close schools and advise people to limit travel and work remotely wherever possible.
